Gandikota Labs: The Half-Built Core

Hyderabad, Sunday 8 February 2026

The generator in the basement of the Gachibowli office cut in at a quarter past ten, and the floor went dark for a second before the lights came back at half brightness. Sruthi Peddireddy, Chief Product Officer of Gandikota Labs, did not look up. On the desk in front of her were two documents she had been alternating between for four hours. The first was a fourteen-page pre-read for the board's technology sub-committee, meeting by video at nine-thirty the next morning with the lead investor dialling in from Bandra Kurla Complex. The second was a single sheet sent at seven that evening without a covering note, listing forty-one code divergences between the master branch of the company's platform and the copies inside four customers' data centres. The delivery director in Chennai had reported fourteen in October. Sruthi had quoted that number, in writing, to the board.

The sub-committee had one agenda item: whether to complete Nava Core, the rebuild of the lending platform approved twenty-one months earlier with a fourteen-month schedule and a ₹9.6 crore budget, on which the company had now spent ₹19.4 crore. Two-fifths of the platform ran on the new core. The rest ran on the old one. Both ran at once, every day, for over a year.

1. The company

Gandikota Labs was founded in Hyderabad in 2016 by Aravind Kuppuswamy, a former payments engineer, and Sruthi's predecessor as head of product, who left in 2022. Its product, Lekka, was a loan management system: the ledger, servicing engine and collections workbench behind a lender's front end, tracking what every borrower owes, when, at what rate, and what happens when they do not pay. Unglamorous infrastructure — and, as the founders correctly guessed, about to be in extraordinary demand, as NBFCs, small finance banks and the first digital lenders found that spreadsheets could not carry a hundred thousand small-ticket loans a month.

Lekka's early advantage was configurability. Indian lending is not one product but hundreds: two-wheeler loans in Coimbatore, gold loans in Thrissur, thirty-day merchant advances against UPI settlement in Indore, co-lending in which an NBFC and a bank each hold a slice of the same loan at different rates. Aravind's team built a rules engine a solution consultant could configure without an engineer, and by 2019 Gandikota was beating Nucleus Software, Jocata and the newer platforms because it could stand up a novel loan product in three weeks.

The decision that constrains everything today was taken in August 2021. Vindhya Capital, a Chennai NBFC and the largest logo Gandikota had pursued, would sign only if Lekka ran inside Vindhya's own data centre, under its own IS audit, with source-code escrow and a right to approve any material architecture change on six months' notice. The board, needing the logo for its Series B, agreed, and three more customers took the same terms over the next two years. Each deployment was branched from the main codebase and then patched in place during two-in-the-morning incidents by engineers who meant to merge the fix upstream next week and sometimes did not. What was sold internally as "four enterprise deployments" was, by 2026, four divergent products with a shared ancestor, and not one sprint had ever gone to reconciling them.

2. The industry

By 2026 the Indian lending-technology market had split into two halves converging awkwardly: the incumbents of regulated infrastructure on one side; on the other, the API-first firms — Lentra, Perfios, FinBox, M2P Fintech, Setu — grown up alongside UPI and the Account Aggregator framework, selling speed rather than depth. Gandikota sat between them: too heavy for a two-week fintech pilot, too light to displace a bank's core.

Regulation shaped the product more than any competitor did. The Reserve Bank of India's digital lending directions made the lender responsible for what its technology partners did with borrower data: Key Fact Statements in a prescribed format, money flowing directly between borrower and lender accounts, limits on what a lending service provider could store. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act added obligations that were, from Sruthi's chair, simply engineering work: consent artefacts, purpose limitation, and a right to erasure honoured across every system holding a borrower's record. Gandikota held copies in eleven places. NPCI's eNACH and UPI Autopay mandates governed how repayments were presented and re-presented; one misreading of a re-presentation window could cost a lender a month of collections and invite a complaint to the RBI ombudsman.

Gandikota's exposure was not only Indian. Its fourth dedicated deployment belonged to Al Yaqeen Finance, a Dubai consumer lender running Lekka on a UAE-resident private cloud, worth ₹11.8 crore a year and bound by residency rules that made the multi-tenant architecture unusable there; its collections peaked sharply around Ramadan, which in 2026 began in the third week of February. Dev Ramaswamy, hired in New Jersey to open a North American book, had two term sheets with US specialty lenders wanting SOC 2 Type II and multi-currency ledgers, neither of which Lekka Classic had.

3. The situation

The Nava Core programme had been approved in May 2024, and the case for it had been, at the time, unanswerable. Exhibit 1 sets out the sequence.

Exhibit 1. Timeline and the prevailing belief at each stage. Compiled by the case writer from board minutes and the Nava Core programme charter.

In the spring of 2024 the pattern was familiar to anyone who had run an ageing platform. A change to interest accrual for one customer surfaced a defect in foreclosure for another, because both read the same denormalised schedule table, and defects had passed half of engineering capacity. Aravind proposed the responsible middle path: not a stop-the-world rewrite but incremental replacement, new services built alongside the old system behind a routing layer, taking one domain at a time until the old system could be switched off. The board approved it; Sruthi, six months into the CPO role, wrote the product plan.

Four assumptions were embedded in that plan; three have since proved wrong. The first was that the domains could be separated cleanly. In practice disbursement, accrual and collections share a mutable loan-state record whose behaviour is defined less by documentation than by twelve years of production data; when the Nava team rebuilt accrual to a specification, four customers found part-prepayment interest had shifted by a few rupees a loan, and two refused the change because their regulatory reporting had been reconciled for years against the old, arguably incorrect, rounding. Nava now carries a compatibility mode reproducing the old behaviour — it carries the debt it was built to retire.

The second assumption was that dedicated deployments would move to the multi-tenant cloud once the RBI's posture on cloud hosting settled. Two mid-sized customers did. Vindhya asked instead for a longer on-premise term; Al Yaqeen cannot move at all, for residency reasons. Exhibit 3 shows what that leaves.

The third assumption was that running both systems would be temporary, so duplication cost could be ignored. Twenty-one months in, duplication is the largest line in the engineering budget (Exhibit 2), and it has not peaked.

The fourth assumption — that the rebuild would make delivery faster — is loudly true in the metrics Aravind shows the board, and the one Sruthi has come to distrust most. Exhibit 4 shows why she distrusts it; Exhibit 5 shows why she cannot prove it.

4. The people

Sruthi Peddireddy — Chief Product Officer, Hyderabad. Owns the recommendation. Publicly she has backed Nava Core in three consecutive board meetings. Privately she believes she approved a fourteen-month estimate she was not qualified to challenge, and she is uncertain whether her instinct to stop the programme is judgement or embarrassment.
Aravind Kuppuswamy — Co-founder and CTO, Bengaluru. Argues Nava is past its hardest phase and that stopping now converts ₹19.4 crore into a write-off and a permanent ceiling on the company. He is not saying that two of his three principal architects have offers from a Bengaluru payments company, nor that his own revised completion estimate differs from the one in the pre-read.
Meenakshi Nair — VP Engineering, Pune, responsible for Lekka Classic. Argues for stopping Nava, folding back the better pieces, and spending eighteen months modularising Classic in place. She has quietly kept a rollback path alive for a year. She is not saying that if Nava proceeds her organisation shrinks from ninety-one engineers to perhaps forty, nor that she was overruled on the original estimate and kept the email.
Farhan Qureshi — Director of Enterprise Delivery, Chennai. Owns the four dedicated deployments. He sent the forty-one-divergence list on Sunday evening; he had reported fourteen in October because fourteen was the number in the tracked register, and a script he ran last week found twenty-seven more. He is not saying that at least six were made by his own team under pressure during a regulatory filing window.
Prakash Menon — Chief Financial Officer, Hyderabad. Has capitalised ₹13.1 crore of Nava development; abandonment impairs that asset this quarter, in the year the board has mandated a path to EBITDA break-even. He frames the choice as financial and commissioned an independent estimate. He is not saying that the acquisition approach received in November values Gandikota on a multiple of earnings, not revenue.
Lea Brandt — Principal Designer, Berlin. Redesigned the collections agent workbench, which exists only on Nava. Her field research in Guntur and Nagpur found agents lose more time to the old keyboard flow than to any outage. She wants Nava finished for reasons that have nothing to do with architecture, and has not reconciled that her sample came from two customers, both on the multi-tenant cloud.
Nikhil Varma — Staff Data Scientist, Toronto. Building a collections-propensity model that the sales team already demonstrates. He argues Nava's event stream is the only viable foundation for it. He has not told the product review that the stream drops roughly nine per cent of events under load, and that his training data is currently backfilled nightly from the Classic database.
Shalini Iyer — Director of Customer Success, Singapore, covering APAC and the Gulf. Manages Al Yaqeen across a ninety-minute gap from Dubai and two and a half hours from Hyderabad. She wants a written commitment that nothing in Al Yaqeen's deployment is touched between 10 February and 30 April. She is not saying that Al Yaqeen's CIO has already asked her, informally, what Gandikota's platform will look like in three years.
Dev Ramaswamy — Head of North America Sales, New Jersey. Has two US term sheets contingent on SOC 2 Type II and multi-currency, and tells anyone who will listen that only Nava can deliver them. Nobody has checked whether the attestation depends on architecture or on controls, and his variable pay is weighted to new-logo bookings this fiscal year.

7. The options as Sruthi currently sees them

A. Complete Nava Core

Fund a further ₹11.5 crore over nine months and hold the line publicly. The argument is that a partial migration is the most expensive state a platform can occupy, and Gandikota pays that cost every month it hesitates. The difficulty is that Aravind's scope, per Exhibit 6, excludes the dedicated deployments entirely: completing Nava on this definition leaves thirty-six per cent of revenue on a system the company has declared obsolete — a harder conversation with Vindhya's board IT committee than with Gandikota's own.

B. Stop Nava and modularise Classic in place

Halt new Nava development, keep the five migrated domains and the co-lending module running, fold the better patterns back into Classic, and spend eighteen months breaking the loan-state record apart inside the existing system. It impairs ₹13.1 crore this quarter, probably costs Aravind and several architects, and asks the board to accept that two years of investment produced one module and a set of lessons. Its defenders say it is the only plan that touches the deployments where the revenue actually is.

C. Freeze both and optimise for earnings

Stop investing in either direction, hold the estate as it is, cut the Nava team, and run the company for cash while the board explores the November approach. Dual-running cost is capped rather than reduced. Nobody will advocate this in the meeting; several people will vote for it in effect, by backing whichever of A or B they believe slowest to start.

Sruthi has written these three into the pre-read. What she has not written, because she cannot yet defend it, is a suspicion that all three share a false premise. Each treats the problem as an architecture problem with a cost and a schedule. Exhibits 3 and 8 can be read as saying something different: that the expensive thing is not the age of the code but the existence of five distinct products sold under one name, and that no rewrite of any kind reduces that number. On that reading the live question is which customers Gandikota intends to serve in 2029 — whether the four dedicated accounts should be priced and staffed as a separate, deliberately frozen business, or divested, or made to pay the true cost of their forks — and the architecture follows from the answer rather than preceding it. Raising it on Monday would mean telling the board that the question it convened to decide is the wrong one, eleven days before Al Yaqeen's peak and three weeks before Vindhya's renewal opens.

8. The deadline and the hard constraints

The sub-committee meets at nine-thirty on Monday 9 February and has asked for a recommendation, not options. Behind it sit constraints that do not negotiate. Cash stands at ₹61 crore against a burn of ₹3.1 crore a month, and the board's FY26 mandate commits the company to EBITDA break-even by the March 2027 quarter; Options A and B each consume most of that headroom. Vindhya's contract requires six months' notice and IS auditor sign-off before any material architecture change, and its renewal opens on 2 March — so a migration decided in February cannot begin before September and cannot be hidden from the renewal. Al Yaqeen's freeze runs through its peak from mid-February. DPDP erasure obligations require a working deletion path across every system holding borrower records by December — eleven deployments, two architectures, forty-one divergences — work absent from both Exhibit 6 estimates. Two principal architects are believed to be in offer processes. The ESOP buyback falls due in June, contingent on the FY26 numbers. And the routing layer that makes dual-running possible is maintained by four engineers, three of them in Pune, reporting to Meenakshi.

9. Questions for discussion

  1. What does Exhibit 4 establish about Gandikota's delivery performance, and what does it not? How should Sruthi present it to a board that has twice seen it without its footnote being read aloud?
  2. Exhibits 4 and 5 point in different directions. Which do you believe, and what single piece of evidence — obtainable within the eleven days before Al Yaqeen's peak — would most change your view?
  3. Each of the eight stakeholders holds a defensible position and withholds something. For Aravind, Meenakshi and Prakash in particular, separate the argument from the incentive. Does knowing the incentive make any of their arguments weaker?
  4. The 2021 decision to accept a customer data-centre deployment was, on the information then available, correct. What would it have taken in 2021 or 2022 to stop it producing forty-one divergences by 2026 — and would the company have survived doing that?
  5. Options A, B and C all frame the choice as rewrite versus build on. State the strongest case that this framing is wrong, what would have to be true of Gandikota's market for the alternative to be right, and what it costs Sruthi personally and politically to raise it.
  6. It is Monday morning. Sruthi has forty minutes and one slide. What does she recommend, what does she tell the board she does not know, and what does she ask them to decide that she cannot decide herself?

Sunday night

At half past eleven the half-lit floor was quiet enough to hear the air-conditioning cycling. The pre-read lay open at page nine, where one line read: Recommendation: continue Nava Core to completion on the revised schedule. She had written it on Thursday, when fourteen was still the number, and had believed it in the way one believes a thing not yet tested.

Her phone showed a message from Shalini in Singapore, an hour old and unanswered, asking whether she could tell Dubai anything before Tuesday. Below it, from Aravind: Can we speak before the call? I want to walk you through my numbers again. Below that, from Meenakshi at 22:48: Whatever you decide tomorrow, decide it. The team can live with either answer. They cannot live with another quarter of both.

Sruthi put the phone face down and looked again at the two documents. The forty-one-line list did not tell her whether to finish the rebuild or stop it. It told her the company had spent twenty-one months deciding without knowing the shape of the thing it was deciding about, and that the meeting in ten hours would be conducted, like the three before it, in numbers whose footnotes nobody would read aloud.

Technical debt: rewrite or build on what we have?

The argument between product and engineering about legacy systems is usually conducted with the wrong unit of account. This is an attempt to set out how the unit should be chosen, what the schools of thought actually disagree about, and which parts of the question remain genuinely unsettled.

OneTwo decisions, two weeks apart

On 4 February 2026, Devika Rao, Chief Product Officer of Baadal Freight Networks, received a one-page memo from her head of platform engineering. Baadal is a Gurugram-based road-freight marketplace: 38,000 verified trucks on one side, 1,900 shipper accounts on the other, ₹1,450 crore of annualised gross booking value at a blended take rate of nine per cent. Seventy-two engineers. The memo asked for fourteen of them, for eleven months, to rewrite the matching service — the code that decides which truck is offered which load at what price.

The supporting numbers were not in dispute. A change to matching logic had a median lead time of 9.5 weeks; a change anywhere else in Baadal's estate took 2.1 weeks. Forty-one per cent of severity-one incidents over the previous year had originated in the matcher. The on-call rotation for that service had been paged 27 times in January. Eleven engineers were assigned to it, and by their own accounting rather more than half their time went to work that the design imposed rather than the roadmap requested. What was in dispute was whether the correct response was to rebuild it or to take it apart.

Eleven days later and 340 kilometres of flight time away, Aparna Deshmukh faced a harder version of the same question at Bakul Health Cloud in Bengaluru. Bakul sells a hospital information system — admissions, orders, results, pharmacy, billing, claims — to forty Indian hospitals, nine of them above 500 beds, ₹78 crore of ARR. Most installations run on the hospital's own infrastructure. Bakul's problem was not a slow service; it was a sentence in its data model written in 2017. An encounter — a patient's episode of care — was modelled as an inpatient admission. Ambulatory and day-care episodes, which are now the faster-growing half of Indian private-hospital volume, are represented as fake admissions with a synthetic discharge six hours later.

The consequences had been arriving for three years. The last six ambulatory features had a median estimate of six weeks and a median actual of seventeen. Claims exports to the National Health Claims Exchange needed per-hospital reconciliation, maintained by a fourteen-person services team in Kochi. Four of nine executive escalations in the previous quarter traced back to the same sentence. Aparna's Chief Technology Officer, Ravi Menon, had proposed what he called a "clean v3" — a new product, new model, migrate everyone over two years.

The two cases share a structure and differ in every constraint that matters. Baadal can move traffic between implementations in seconds, but its system's behaviour determines who earns money. Bakul can define correct behaviour precisely, but cannot move a single hospital without that hospital's consent, its medical records officer's sign-off and a maintenance window agreed six weeks in advance. Held together, they expose most of what is worth knowing about the subject.

TwoThe idea, its history, and who disagrees about it

Technical debt is the difference between the design a system has and the design its builders would now choose, valued by what that difference costs to work around. The metaphor is Ward Cunningham's, from a short experience report delivered at the OOPSLA conference in 1992 about a portfolio-management product called WyCash. His claim was narrow and is often misquoted: shipping code is like borrowing, because it lets you learn sooner than you otherwise could; the borrowing is prudent only if you rework the code as the learning arrives. In a 2009 video he stated the negative case directly — the metaphor was never a licence to write code badly. The debt is the lag between understanding and design, and the interest is what you pay every time you touch the lagging design.

Two structural additions turned the metaphor into something usable. Martin Fowler's debt quadrant (2009) separates deliberate from inadvertent and prudent from reckless, which disentangles a moral question from an economic one. Michael Feathers, in Working Effectively with Legacy Code (2004), supplied the operational definition that most practitioners now use without attribution: legacy code is code without tests, and the craft of changing it consists of finding seams — places where behaviour can be substituted without editing the code you are afraid of. Fowler's strangler fig pattern (2004) gave the replacement strategy its canonical form. Behind all of it sits Manny Lehman's laws of software evolution, formulated across the 1970s from observation of IBM's OS/360: a system in use must keep changing or become progressively less useful, and its complexity increases with change unless work is done explicitly to reduce it. Debt, in Lehman's framing, is not an accident. It is the default state of any system that is still worth using.

What follows from that history is a set of positions that are frequently treated as one consensus and are not. The table below states, for each, the proposition it would sign and the adjacent proposition it would refuse — which is the faster way to tell them apart.

Five positions on technical debt that are routinely conflated. Competent practitioners hold different ones; the arguments in most engineering all-hands are between these rows rather than between individuals.
PositionWould signWould not signRests on
Original / CunninghamDebt is design lag created by learning; repay it continuously through refactoring as understanding improves."Technical debt means the bad code we knowingly wrote to hit a date."The observation that requirements are only understood after a first version exists.
Never rewrite / SpolskyWorking code embodies years of discovered edge cases; discarding it destroys information you cannot recover cheaply."A clean architecture is worth a year away from the market."Netscape's rewrite and the market position lost with it; Apple's Copland; a long list of unfinished v2s.
Incrementalist / Fowler, FeathersAny replacement must be delivered in slices behind a seam, with the old system live until the new one has earned each slice."We will add the characterisation tests once the new system is finished."Repeated success of strangler-fig migrations; repeated failure of parallel builds.
Options / Matts and FreemanDebt is the wrong metaphor: unrepaid design lag behaves like an unhedged call option written against you — cost unbounded, exercised at the worst moment."We can schedule the repayment for next year and the cost will be roughly what it is today."The empirical shape of legacy incidents: rare, correlated with growth, and catastrophic.

There is a sixth position, held with some force and worth stating separately because it denies the premise of the whole argument: that the trade-off between internal quality and delivery speed is largely illusory past a horizon of a few weeks. Fowler's "design stamina hypothesis" and the DORA research programme's finding that throughput and stability move together rather than against each other both point this way. If that view is right, then debating how much debt to take is like debating how much sand to put in the fuel tank. We will return to it, because it is the disagreement with the largest practical consequences.

ThreeMechanics, including the parts left implicit

Expert practice has four moves. Two of them are widely described. The two in the middle are where most of the value is, and they are usually performed tacitly by one senior engineer whose reasoning nobody writes down.

Move one: denominate everything in engineer-weeks

Baadal's fully loaded cost is ₹42 lakh per engineer per year over a 46-week working year: ₹0.91 lakh per engineer-week. Bakul's, in Bengaluru with a more junior mix, is ₹30 lakh, or ₹0.65 lakh per engineer-week. Converting every claim into this unit is not accounting pedantry; it is what makes the arguments commensurable. "The matcher is a mess" and "we need three more salespeople" cannot be compared. "The matcher costs 304 engineer-weeks a year" and "three salespeople cost ₹96 lakh" can.

Move two: separate interest from ugliness, by classification not by opinion

Interest is capacity consumed by work that would not exist if the design were right. Baadal classified six months of completed work items into three buckets: outcomes a customer or a trucker would notice; work forced by the design — the same change made in three places, manual regression because there is no harness, incidents with a known structural cause; and everything else. The boundary is arguable and the argument is productive: it is the first conversation in which the PM and the tech lead have to agree what the design is costing rather than how it feels. Baadal's result: 304 engineer-weeks a year, ₹2.77 crore, or 9.2 per cent of the entire engineering budget spent on one service's design lag.

Move three: find the concentration — the step usually left implicit

Debt is never uniform. Intersecting change frequency from version control with defect incidence from the incident log — the technique Adam Tornhill popularised as behavioural code analysis — reliably shows a few per cent of files absorbing a large majority of both. Baadal's matcher is 61,000 lines; 4,100 of them, in three files, accounted for 58 per cent of commits and 71 per cent of defects in the service. Everything else in the service was stable.

Move four: attach a maturity, then choose the smallest reversible slice

Each item needs an estimated remaining maturity: how long the code stays on the roadmap's critical path. Interest on a short-dated item is close to free, and deliberately defaulting on it is correct. Baadal's legacy GPS adapter is genuinely terrible and is scheduled for retirement when the last two telematics vendors are consolidated in 2027; touching it would destroy value. Once interest, principal and maturity are on the page, the choice among strategies is nearly mechanical — and the strategies are not two but six, which is itself most of the PM's contribution to the meeting.

They are: containment (wrap it in an interface, freeze it, build outside); refactoring (change internal structure, preserve observable behaviour, ship continuously); parallel change, also called expand–contract (add the new shape beside the old, migrate readers and writers, remove the old); strangler-fig replacement (new implementation beside the old behind a router, traffic moved in slices, old deleted); re-platforming (same code, new infrastructure); and big-bang rewrite (build the whole replacement, cut over once). The mechanics that experts execute and novices omit sit inside the middle two: a router or facade at the seam; shadow mode, in which the new path processes live traffic but its output is discarded and compared; a reconciliation harness that logs every divergence with enough context to adjudicate it; a percentage or partition-based cutover; and — the step most often skipped — a dated, owned decommissioning of the old code. A replacement that reaches 100 per cent of traffic but never deletes the original has raised the cost of the system rather than lowered it.

Baadal's three options can be valued properly. Take a 25 per cent discount rate — high, reflecting a growth-stage marketplace's cost of capital and the genuine probability that the matching problem is different in four years — and let interest grow 12 per cent annually with volume if nothing is done. FourWhen the frame applies, and when it misleads

The debt frame rests on four conditions. Stated as testable claims, they can be checked against each protagonist in an afternoon.

Claim one: the code will still be on the critical path long enough for compounding to matter. True at Baadal for lane pricing — freight matching is the product and will be for a decade. Ambiguously true at Bakul: the encounter model will outlive everyone in the building, so its maturity is effectively infinite, which makes Bakul's case for remediation stronger than Baadal's even though its interest bill is smaller. False for a pre-product-market-fit start-up where the median module has a life expectancy of eleven months.

Claim two: the interest is measurable and attributable. True at Baadal, where work items map cleanly to services. Partly false at Bakul, where the largest single cost — ₹1.46 crore a year of the Kochi services team's reconciliation work — appears on the services P&L, not engineering's. A PM reading only engineering's numbers would price Bakul's debt at roughly half its true cost. This is the most common systematic error in B2B software.

Claim three: a seam exists, or can be created for less than the remediation itself. True at Baadal: requests already pass through an API gateway, so a router can be inserted in days. Harder at Bakul, where the data model is the seam — there is no interface to hide behind, which is why data-model debt is categorically more expensive than service-boundary debt and why the frame's usual advice ("slice it") needs a different technique here.

Claim four: the domain is stable enough that today's target design will still be the target when you arrive. This is the condition that most often fails silently. A team that spends nine months rebuilding to a specification of the problem that was correct in February will arrive in November with a beautifully engineered answer to a question the market has moved past.

The frame is actively misleading in three situations. When the real constraint is flow rather than code — when a feature has three weeks of work and eleven weeks of elapsed time, and the missing eight are queueing for review, environments, dependent teams and decisions — debt remediation will consume a year and change nothing measurable. When the argument is really about morale, autonomy or on-call pain, the debt vocabulary lets both sides avoid the actual conversation; the tell is a proposal whose benefits are all stated in architectural nouns. And when a company's survival horizon is shorter than the payback period, the correct discount rate makes almost all remediation irrational, which is why advice calibrated for a 600-person firm can be actively harmful in a 15-person one.

FiveHard cases: where the standard answer breaks

Two-sided markets. Baadal's matcher does not merely compute; it allocates income. Its accumulated quirks — a preference for trucks with recent completions on the lane, a rounding rule that favours returns-leg pricing — have become the rules by which 38,000 owner operators plan their weeks. A "correct" replacement is a market redesign. Two consequences follow that a single-sided product never faces. Percentage-based cutover is contaminated: truckers on the new matcher and truckers on the old compete for the same loads, so the experiment interferes with its own control. Baadal's answer was to cut over by lane — Gurugram–Jaipur first, a geographically isolable sub-market — accepting less statistical power in exchange for a clean unit of analysis. And bug-for-bug compatibility becomes an explicit commercial decision: Devika's team had to enumerate, behaviour by behaviour, which quirks were contract and which were accident, then price the goodwill cost of changing the second kind.

Regulated and on-premise enterprise. Bakul cannot cut anything over. Upgrades are scheduled by the customer, validated by the hospital's medical records officer, and constrained by the audit requirements attaching to clinical records and to claims filed through the national exchange. Bakul's historical adoption of major versions is 62 per cent at eighteen months. That single number destroys the "clean v3" proposal arithmetically: a new product implies running two products for at least three years, with two compliance surfaces, two support teams and a services organisation that must know both. The same number makes parallel change attractive, because expand–contract can be performed inside a version that hospitals adopt for other reasons — the migration rides along with features they want.

Hardware plus software. Bhaskar Instruments, in Coimbatore, sells connected water-quality meters to municipal utilities and industrial users: 34,000 units in the field, of which about nine per cent sit on networks that have not called home in over a year. Its cloud platform can be strangled like any other service. Its device firmware cannot: an over-the-air update that bricks a meter in a treatment plant is a truck roll and a safety conversation, and the units that never connect will run the 2019 protocol until they are physically replaced. Bhaskar's debt on the device protocol therefore has effectively infinite maturity and no available remediation. The only correct strategy is containment: a translation layer in the cloud that isolates the old protocol forever, priced as a permanent operating cost rather than a project.

AI-native products. At Ghanaakshar Labs in Chennai, which extracts structured data from lending documents, roughly forty per cent of what functions as the system is not conventional code at all: prompts, retrieval index schemas, evaluation sets and the labelling conventions behind them. Debt accumulates in the eval set faster than in the code — 180 hand-labelled documents chosen in 2024 no longer represent the distribution of what customers send, so the team's measurements are confidently wrong. Two structural differences follow. First, this debt has an externally imposed due date: when a model vendor announces a deprecation with nine months' notice, a migration the company did not choose becomes mandatory, which is the opposite of the usual situation in which debt can be deferred indefinitely. Second, assistant-generated code has raised the rate at which code is produced without raising the rate at which it is understood, shifting the bottleneck from writing to reviewing and — in the view of several practitioners, though the evidence is still thin — accelerating debt accumulation precisely in the systems where remediation is cheapest to automate.

Multi-product estates and the organisational seams. The hardest cases are not technical. When debt sits in a shared library used by four product teams, the interest is paid by all of them and the remediation must be funded by one; in the absence of an explicit mechanism this is a commons problem and it resolves the way commons problems resolve. When a platform team is chartered to build the replacement while product teams keep shipping on the original, Conway's law does the rest: two systems, two constituencies, and a migration that never completes because nobody with power is inconvenienced by its incompleteness. Mature companies handle this less elegantly than their conference talks suggest. What actually works, where it works, is embarrassingly mundane: the team that owns the old system owns the replacement; the migration is funded as a line item with a named executive sponsor; and someone senior is personally accountable for the deletion date.

SixNine distinctions an expert makes and a competent practitioner does not

Interest is paid first in variance, then in the mean

Before median cycle times rise, estimate spread widens: the same team that used to say "three weeks, give or take three days" starts saying "three to nine weeks". The expert tell is a team that has begun padding uniformly rather than estimating — a sign that engineers can no longer predict what a change will touch. By the time medians move, the condition has been present for two or three quarters.

The visible debt is rarely the expensive debt

Ugly code announces itself; a data model that cannot represent the domain does not, because its cost appears as unrelated symptoms — reconciliation scripts, support escalations, analytics that nobody trusts, a services team that keeps growing. Experts triangulate from the symptoms backward. Aparna found Bakul's real debt not in an architecture review but by asking why the Kochi team had grown from four people to fourteen while customer count grew by nine.

Debt is a property of code and roadmap jointly

The same code carries different debt in two companies with different plans. This is why "how much technical debt do we have?" has no answer and "what did our design cost us last quarter, and what will it cost the next four things on the roadmap?" has a good one. The tell of someone who has internalised this: they ask to see the roadmap before they look at the code.

Rewrites fail at requirements archaeology, not at engineering

The difficulty in replacing a mature system is establishing what it does and which of those behaviours are contractual. That is product work, and when a PM describes the rewrite as an engineering matter they have removed the one person whose job it is to adjudicate the question. The expert tell is a replacement plan with a named product owner and a budget line for behaviour discovery — reading support tickets, interviewing operations staff, instrumenting the old system to find out which code paths are actually executed.

Not all slowness is debt; most of it is queueing

Value-stream measurement repeatedly finds touch time to be a minority of elapsed time. A team whose eleven-week lead time is eight weeks of waiting will not be helped by a better codebase. The diagnostic is cheap: take the last ten completed items, mark for each the hours of hands-on work and the calendar days elapsed, and look at the ratio. Experts run this before agreeing to a remediation programme, and are unsurprised when it kills one.

Bug-for-bug compatibility is a product decision

Every replacement must decide which observable behaviours are contract and which are accident, and only the product side can decide. At Baadal this is unusually stark because the accidents redistribute income, but it is true everywhere: the enterprise customer who built a macro around an oddly formatted export is relying on an accident that has become a contract. The expert artefact is a behaviour register with two columns, produced before any code is written.

Debt has a term structure, and defaulting can be correct

The competent practitioner sorts remediation candidates by how bad they are. The expert sorts by interest × remaining maturity and immediately strikes out everything short-dated, however offensive. This usually removes a third of the list and is the fastest way to convert a demoralising backlog into a fundable plan.

When engineers ask for a rewrite, find out what they are asking for

A rewrite request is sometimes a request for a rewrite. It is at least as often a request for relief from on-call pain, for autonomy, for work that is legible to a future employer, or for the chance to use a technology the market now rewards. None of these are illegitimate, and all of them have cheaper solutions than eleven months of rebuilding. The tell is a proposal whose benefits are expressed entirely in architectural nouns — microservices, event sourcing, type safety — with no sentence beginning "so that we can".

Reversibility dominates total cost

Given two plans, one costing 264 engineer-weeks with a decision point every ten weeks and one costing 200 with a single decision point at the start, experts take the more expensive plan almost without argument. The reason is visible in the Baadal table: the value of the strangler is not that it is cheaper if everything goes as expected, but that it is nearly as good if you stop halfway. In a domain where forecasts are unreliable, optionality is worth more than efficiency.

SevenHow the decision differs by product type and company stage

Some of the variation across product types is real and some of it is folklore. The real differences are three. In consumer products the interest is usually paid in learning rate rather than in engineer-weeks: Ghazal Audio, a Hyderabad streaming service with eleven million monthly listeners, can ship a feature quickly but cannot run two variants of its player at once, so it manages 38 experiments a quarter where a better-instrumented competitor manages three times as many. No time-tracking exercise will surface that cost, and no engineer will report it, because from inside the team nothing feels slow.

In B2B and enterprise the interest migrates onto other teams' budgets — services, implementation, support — and the debt is concentrated in configurability rather than in core logic. In marketplaces and platforms the debt is entangled with market outcomes and with third-party developers, which converts engineering choices into commercial negotiations and makes bug-for-bug compatibility expensive to abandon and expensive to keep. In hardware, some debt simply cannot be repaid and must be contained and funded forever. In AI-native products, some debt comes with an external due date set by a vendor's deprecation schedule.

What does not differ, and is often claimed to: the underlying analysis. Interest, principal, maturity, seam, slice. Anyone who tells you that marketplaces need a fundamentally different theory of technical debt is describing a difference in the inputs, not in the method.

Stage changes the discount rate, and the discount rate changes everything. A fifteen-person company with eighteen months of runway should take deliberate debt freely, because the probability that any given module still matters when the debt comes due is low, and slowness now is existential. By Series B, with contractual customers and a two-year horizon, the calculus begins to invert. In a 600-person organisation the debt is paid by teams that did not take it, in code they did not write, and compounding runs for a decade; here the error is almost always under-investment, and the correct posture is a standing programme rather than a project. The sharpest observable difference: small companies should record the debt they take deliberately and rarely do; large companies should delete the debt they have already remediated around and almost never do.

EightThree worked cases, one of them a failure

Case one: Baadal, lane pricing, strangled in four slices

Slice one took six engineers ten weeks — 60 engineer-weeks, ₹54.8 lakh. The new pricing component handled spot loads on four northern lanes, about three per cent of volume, and ran in shadow mode for the first three weeks: live inputs, outputs discarded and compared against the old path, every divergence logged with the load's characteristics. The reconciliation harness found 2,140 divergences in week one. Nine hundred were rounding. Two hundred and six were the old system being wrong in ways nobody had noticed. The remainder were the behaviours Devika's team then had to classify as contract or accident — the single most valuable artefact the project produced, and one a big-bang rewrite would have generated only at cutover, under pressure, at scale. By slice three, interest on lane pricing had fallen from 176 engineer-weeks a year to 41, and the median lead time for a pricing change was 2.4 weeks.

Case two: Bakul, the encounter model, expanded and contracted

Aparna did not get Ravi's clean v3. She got 270 engineer-weeks over seven months to add the new episode representation beside the old, dual-write everything, and backfill 2.3 crore historical rows hospital by hospital. The business case rested on two numbers: the ambulatory feature multiple, which she expected to fall from 2.8× the original estimate to about 1.2×, and the Kochi reconciliation load, ₹1.46 crore a year of which she projected recovering ₹1.05 crore once nine bespoke scripts per hospital collapsed into one. Payback on ₹2.07 crore of total project cost: a shade under two years — poor by start-up standards, entirely normal for enterprise software with a ten-year product life and a customer base that renews at 94 per cent. The condition she attached was the one that mattered: no new module could read the old tables from month eight, and the contract phase had a date, an owner and a bonus attached.

Case three: Basera Living, and what a failure actually costs

Basera Living rents furniture and appliances to urban households and runs the associated service network. In March 2024 it began a fourteen-month rewrite of its order-to-fulfilment stack: 22 engineers, a new architecture, and a plan whose first customer-visible milestone sat in month twelve. It was cancelled in month eleven with ₹6.8 crore spent.

The proximate cause was requirements archaeology. The old system contained roughly 2,400 conditional branches, a large share of which encoded city-level operational reality — which Bengaluru pin codes the two-wheeler fleet could serve, how Delhi NCR inter-state movements generated e-way bill obligations, which buildings in south Mumbai required a service lift booking 48 hours ahead. The rewrite team, reasonably, treated these as noise. They were the product. The deeper cause was structural: with no incremental delivery, there was no month in which anyone could compare the new system to the old on evidence, so the decision to continue was re-taken every month on faith, and the political cost of stopping rose with every crore spent. Cancelling at month four would have cost ₹2.4 crore; cancelling at month eleven cost ₹6.8 crore plus seven of twenty-two engineers within two quarters, which was the more expensive half of the loss.

The recovery is the instructive part. Basera's new head of engineering wrapped the legacy system in an anti-corruption layer — a translation boundary that lets new code speak a clean vocabulary while the old code keeps its own — and ported the one genuinely finished component, the pricing service, behind it in seven weeks. She then ran a hotspot analysis, found that three files carried most of the change and most of the defects, and spent ₹48 lakh remediating them. Cycle time improved 31 per cent in two quarters. The ₹6.8 crore was not entirely wasted: the behaviour catalogue the rewrite team had built became the specification for everything that followed. But it is a costly way to buy a specification.

TenWhere competent people genuinely disagree

Is the quality–speed trade-off real at all?

The strong version of the quality-is-free position holds that beyond a horizon of a few weeks there is no trade: high internal quality makes delivery faster, not slower, and the DORA research programme's repeated finding that throughput and stability correlate positively is offered as evidence. Steelmanned, this is not a claim that speed does not matter; it is a claim that the apparent saving from cutting corners is realised within days and reversed within weeks, so a manager who believes they are buying time is mispricing an exchange rate. The opposing position, held by many people who have actually run seed-stage companies, is that the relevant horizon is sometimes shorter than the payback: if a company dies in nine months, quality investment with a fourteen-week payback is a luxury it cannot buy. For the first view to be wrong, you would need cases where sustained corner-cutting produced durable advantage; for the second to be wrong, you would need to show that the companies that died did not die of slowness. Both bodies of evidence are contaminated by survivorship, and the disagreement is not close to settled.

Should debt work be budgeted, or invisible?

One camp wants an explicit allocation — twenty per cent, a standing platform team, a visible register — on the grounds that what is not funded does not happen and that executives cannot govern what they cannot see. The other camp, descending from the "boy scout rule", holds that any separate budget is a signal that debt work is optional, and that the only sustainable practice is remediation folded into the estimate of every feature that touches the affected code. The second position has the better theory and the worse empirical record in large organisations, where estimates are negotiated downward by people who cannot see what was removed. The first has the better record and creates the theatre described above. Practitioners who have watched both fail tend to converge on a hybrid — named items with named outcomes rather than a percentage — but that is a truce rather than a resolution.

Can debt be measured, or only its symptoms?

The portfolio school argues for explicit measurement: principal estimates, interest attribution, hotspot analysis, indices computed from static analysis. The sceptics reply that every such measure is a proxy that will be optimised directly once it is managed, and that the only honest measurement is the lead time of the next real change. The sceptics are plainly right about gaming and plainly wrong that judgement scales: a 600-person organisation cannot run on one principal engineer's intuition. What would settle it is evidence that measured programmes outperform unmeasured ones at constant spend, and that evidence does not exist in any form that would survive scrutiny.

Is a big-bang rewrite ever correct?

The incrementalists' claim is close to universal: there is always a seam, and if there is not, creating one is cheaper than rebuilding. The counter-position — argued most persuasively by people who have replaced data models rather than services — is that some constraints are representational. If the domain cannot be expressed in the existing model at all, then every incremental step must carry a translation, the translations accumulate, and the cost of the incremental path can exceed the rewrite. Bakul is the interesting test: Ravi Menon's clean v3 was defeated not by the incrementalist argument but by a customer-adoption number. Had Bakul been fully multi-tenant and cloud-hosted, with cutover under its own control, the calculation might genuinely have gone the other way, and the honest conclusion is that the never-rewrite rule is a very good heuristic derived from a world of high migration costs rather than a law.

What do coding assistants do to all of this?

This is the live disagreement of 2026 and the one with the least evidence behind either position. One view: the cost of a rewrite has fallen materially, because porting logic between languages and generating characterisation tests for untested code are exactly the tasks the current generation of models does well, so the never-rewrite heuristic — which was always a statement about cost — should be loosened. The other: assistants have raised the volume of code produced without raising the volume understood, and debt is a function of understanding, so the same tools that make remediation cheaper make accumulation faster, with the net effect negative in precisely the systems that are already hardest to reason about. Both positions are held by serious people. What would settle it is a few years of data on defect rates and change costs in heavily assisted codebases, and that data does not yet exist.

ElevenWhat mastery looks like in practice

Someone who has merely studied this topic can define debt, name the quadrant and describe the strangler fig. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in four observable ways.

They change the unit of the argument before engaging with it. Presented with "we need to rewrite the matcher", their first move is not to agree or refuse but to ask which files, which roadmap items, and what last quarter cost — converting a binary question into a portfolio one, which is where the good answers live. They are comfortable saying "that module is terrible and we are never going to fix it", because they have a maturity estimate and are not confusing engineering aesthetics with economics. They treat reversibility as the dominant criterion, preferring the more expensive plan with more exit points, and they can explain why in the language of the finance function rather than of architecture. And they hold the deletion date personally, because they have learned that the failure mode which costs the most is not the rewrite that collapses but the replacement that succeeds and never removes what it replaced.

There is a fifth, subtler marker. They are willing to spend product management's own capacity on behaviour discovery — reading four years of support tickets, sitting with the operations team in Bhiwandi, instrumenting the old system to find which branches actually execute — rather than delegating it to engineers who will reasonably treat the exceptions as noise. Basera Living's ₹6.8 crore was, in the end, the price of nobody doing that work in month one.

TwelveWhat each of them decided

Devika Rao declined the eleven-month rewrite on 19 February 2026 and funded a first slice of ten weeks against lane pricing, with three conditions: shadow mode before any live traffic, a divergence dashboard reviewed weekly by a product manager rather than an engineer, and a cutover sequenced by lane rather than by percentage of users because of the market-interference problem. Her stated reason to the board was the asymmetry in the table: a strangler abandoned halfway is worth almost as much as one completed, and a rewrite abandoned halfway is worth nothing.

Aparna Deshmukh declined the clean v3 on the strength of a single number — 62 per cent adoption of major versions at eighteen months, implying at least three years of running two products — and funded a parallel-change remediation of the encounter model, with the contract phase dated and owned before phase one began. She accepted, publicly, that ambulatory features would remain expensive for a further eight months, and negotiated the roadmap accordingly rather than concealing it.

Discussion questions.

1. Baadal's strangler stopped after slice two has a four-year present value almost identical to the completed version. If that is true, why fund slices three and four at all — and what would have to be true about the numbers for stopping to be the better decision?

2. Bakul's largest single interest payment sits on the services P&L in Kochi, where no engineering leader is accountable for it. Whose problem is that, and what mechanism would you build so that the next instance is found in month three rather than year three?

3. Ravi Menon's clean v3 was rejected on a customer-adoption number, not on an engineering argument. Suppose Bakul had been fully multi-tenant and cloud-hosted, with migration under its own control. Would the rejection still have been right, and what does your answer imply about how much of the never-rewrite doctrine is a statement about software and how much about distribution?

ThirteenGoing deeper

The software development lifecycle is where this topic's premise comes from: debt accumulates across cycles, and understanding how requirements, build, test and release actually sequence tells you where the lag enters. Cost, quality and time trade-offs is the general form of the argument made here in a special case; it supplies the vocabulary for the disagreement in section ten. Migrations and rebuilds is the operational sequel — dual-write, backfill, reconciliation, cutover and decommissioning are where replacement projects actually die, and the detail matters more than the strategy. Strategic debt takes the opposite side seriously: how to borrow deliberately, price the borrowing at the moment you take it, and leave a record for whoever inherits it.

Agile in practice and Kanban and flow both bear on the queueing diagnostic: if most of your lead time is waiting rather than working, these tell you how to see it and what to do. The execution rhythm determines whether the debt register is reviewed monthly alongside the roadmap or quietly in an engineering forum, which in practice determines whether it is funded. Engineering estimates and T-shirt sizing is the topic that explains the variance signal in section nine — why spread widens before medians move, and how to read padding as information rather than as evasion. Backlog management and refinement is where behaviour discovery for a replacement either happens or does not. And definition of done is the quiet lever: a definition that includes tests, instrumentation and the removal of what the change superseded is the single most effective control on the rate at which new debt accumulates — which is, over a ten-year product life, worth considerably more than any remediation programme.

Technical debt: rewrite or build on what we have?

A working guide to the oldest argument between product managers and engineers — what debt actually is, how to price it, and why the honest answer is almost never the one either side walks into the room holding.

OnePune, March 2026: eleven weeks to add a picking rule

Ananya Kulkarni had been Vice-President of Product at Bhramar Systems for nineteen months when the argument finally became a decision. Bhramar sells warehouse management software to mid-market Indian retailers and third-party logistics operators — the software that tells a picker in a Bhiwandi warehouse which shelf to walk to, in which order, and which carton to put the goods in. Its customers are suppliers to the large retail chains, sellers who fulfil for Flipkart and Amazon, and a growing set of quick-commerce dark-store operators. Ninety-one customers, ₹94 crore of annual recurring revenue, sixty-four people in engineering.

The trigger was a deal. A quick-commerce operator wanted a picking strategy Bhramar did not have: batch-picking across multiple small orders with a ten-minute promise. Nikhil Barve, Bhramar's Director of Engineering, estimated eleven weeks. Ananya had watched the same team build an entirely new returns module, from blank page to production, in four. The difference was not the difficulty of batch-picking. The difference was that picking strategies lived inside the allocation engine — 140,000 lines of Java written in 2016 by two engineers who had since left, with no automated tests, three forked copies of the pricing logic, and configuration for each customer expressed as rows in a table that only one person, a principal engineer in Hyderabad named Farida Sheikh, could read confidently.

Nikhil's proposal was nine months and six engineers to rewrite the engine. Sudha Iyer, the chief executive, asked the question that chief executives ask: "And during those nine months, what do we ship?" Nikhil said the roadmap would be thin. Ananya had four competitive deals in the pipeline that turned on features the roadmap would no longer contain. If she said no, the eleven-week cycle time stayed and every future deal took the same hit. If she said yes and the rewrite ran long — as the last one at her previous employer had, by seven months — Bhramar would spend a year producing nothing a customer could see, in a market where two well-funded competitors were shipping monthly.

This is the classic conflict, and the reason it is classic is that both parties are usually right about the facts and wrong about the frame.

TwoWhat technical debt actually means

Technical debt is the gap between the design a system has and the design its builders would choose today, measured by what that gap costs to work around. The term comes from Ward Cunningham, a programmer who in 1992 wrote a short experience report about building a financial product called WyCash. Shipping code that does not yet match your understanding of the problem, he wrote, is like going into debt: a little debt speeds development up, provided you repay it promptly by reworking the code as your understanding improves. Every minute spent on code that is not quite right counts as interest.

Cunningham was later explicit, in a 2009 interview, that people had misread him. He did not mean "writing bad code on purpose." He meant the perfectly normal condition in which you learn what the software should have been only after you have written it. The debt is the design lag. The interest is what you pay, in engineer-hours, every time you touch the lagging design.

Two clarifications are worth having ready, because they are what separate someone who understands the idea from someone repeating the word. The first is Martin Fowler's 2009 debt quadrant: debt can be deliberate or inadvertent, and prudent or reckless, and these are independent. Deliberate-and-prudent debt ("we know this won't scale past 200 warehouses; we'll be back before then") is a legitimate, often correct, product decision. Inadvertent-and-prudent debt ("now that it's built, we see how we should have built it") is Cunningham's original case and is unavoidable. Reckless debt of either kind is just poor work, and calling it debt flatters it.

The second clarification is the one Ananya needed for the meeting: debt is a property of a system and a roadmap together, never of code alone. Ugly code in a module nobody will touch again costs nothing. Elegant code in a module you must change weekly can still be expensive if the elegance is in the wrong shape. This gives the sentence she could repeat without sounding glib: "The question isn't whether the code is bad. The question is what interest we're paying on each part of it, and how long we intend to keep holding that part."

ThreeHow the decision actually works

Practitioners who are good at this run four steps, of which the middle two are usually left implicit and are where the argument is really won.

Step one: measure the interest, not the ugliness. Interest is engineering capacity consumed by work that would disappear if the design were right. It is observable. Ananya asked Nikhil's team to classify six months of completed work into three buckets: work a customer would notice, work forced on them by the design (duplicated changes across forks, manual regression testing where a test suite should exist, firefighting incidents traceable to a known structural cause), and everything else. That classification is imperfect — engineers argue about the boundary — but it is an order of magnitude better than asking "how bad is the code?", which has no answer.

Step two: find the concentration. Debt is never evenly spread. In almost every system, a small fraction of files absorbs most of the change and most of the defects. You find them by intersecting two facts both freely available from version control and the incident log: how often each area changes, and how often it breaks. Areas that are ugly but static are not worth touching. Areas that are ugly and change every week are where the money is.

Step three: attach a maturity to each item. Ask, for each candidate, how long the code will remain on the roadmap's critical path. A module you plan to replace in two quarters for product reasons has near-zero remaining maturity, and you should default on its debt deliberately. A module that will sit under every feature for the next four years has a long maturity and compounding matters.

Step four: choose the smallest reversible slice. The options are not "rewrite" and "live with it". There are at least five, and naming them precisely is most of the PM's contribution to the conversation. Refactoring means changing internal structure without changing observable behaviour, in small steps, while continuing to ship. Re-platforming means moving the same code to different infrastructure. Strangler-fig replacement — Fowler's 2004 coinage, after the fig that grows around a host tree until the tree can be removed — means building the new implementation beside the old one, routing a slice of traffic to it, and expanding the slice until the old one can be deleted. Big-bang rewrite means building a replacement in parallel and cutting over at the end. Containment means writing an interface around the bad module, freezing it, and building everything new outside it.

FourThe arithmetic, worked

Bhramar's engineering cost is ₹28 lakh per engineer per year fully loaded, across a 46-working-week year. That is ₹0.61 lakh per engineer-week — the unit in which this decision is best denominated, because it converts every argument into the same currency. The allocation engine team is nine engineers: 9 × 46 = 414 engineer-weeks a year, or ₹2.52 crore.

The classification exercise put the debt interest at 39 per cent of those 414 weeks: 62 weeks of incident firefighting with a structural root cause, 48 weeks making the same change three times across three forks of the pricing code, and 51 weeks of manual regression testing that a test suite would remove. That is 161 engineer-weeks, or ₹98 lakh a year, paid every year, growing.

Now price Nikhil's rewrite. Six engineers for nine months is 6 × 39 = 234 engineer-weeks, or ₹1.43 crore. Bhramar's own history suggests projects of this shape have overrun by about 1.8×; applying that multiplier gives 421 engineer-weeks, or ₹2.57 crore. Assume optimistically that the rewrite removes 80 per cent of the interest — 129 weeks, ₹79 lakh a year saved. At the optimistic cost, payback is 1.43 ÷ 0.79 = 1.8 years. At the historically honest cost, 2.57 ÷ 0.79 = 3.3 years. And for the first nine to sixteen months of that, the roadmap is thin, which is a separate cost Ananya can size: the four deals at risk represent ₹3.1 crore of new ARR.

Then change one input, and watch the decision invert. Ask not what the interest is in aggregate but where it is concentrated. When the team tagged those 161 weeks by module, 124 of them — 77 per cent — came from one component: strategy selection, roughly 11,000 of the 140,000 lines. The rest of the engine was dull, stable and cheap to live with.

The register does the work that the aggregate hid. Replacing strategy selection alone — three engineers, twenty weeks, 60 engineer-weeks, ₹36.6 lakh — removes an estimated 100 of the 124 interest-weeks, ₹61 lakh a year. Payback is seven months, and the roadmap stays open because six of nine engineers keep shipping. The same project that looked marginal at ₹2.57 crore looks obvious at ₹36.6 lakh, and the difference is entirely a matter of choosing the right unit of decision. The unit is never "the system". It is always a module, a seam and a slice of traffic.

FiveThe nuances that separate understanding from vocabulary

Interest is felt; principal is not

You never experience the principal — the total cost of fixing everything — because you never pay it all at once. You experience interest, one delayed feature at a time. This is why teams consistently under-react: each individual payment is small enough to absorb, and the compounding is invisible until a chart like the one above is drawn. It is also why "how big is our debt?" is an unanswerable question and "what did debt cost us last quarter?" is a good one.

Debt has a term structure

Every item has a remaining maturity, and interest on a short-maturity item is nearly free. Bhramar's legacy reporting module is genuinely awful; it is also being replaced for product reasons within two quarters. Spending eighty engineer-weeks making it beautiful would be a straightforward destruction of ₹49 lakh. Knowing when to deliberately default on debt is as much a part of this skill as knowing when to repay.

Ugly code often encodes knowledge you cannot see

Joel Spolsky's argument in 2000, written after watching Netscape rewrite its browser and lose its market position, remains the strongest case against rewrites: the messy conditionals in old code are usually bug fixes, each representing something learned about the real world at some cost. Bhramar's allocation engine contains 2,400 branches; a fair number encode the behaviour of specific customers' physical warehouses — a mezzanine floor in Bhiwandi that cannot take a pallet jack, a Chennai site where the GST e-way bill print station sits at the wrong end of the dock. A rewrite that does not recover those facts will rediscover them in production, one escalation at a time.

Rewrites fail at requirements archaeology, not at engineering

Related, but distinct, and it changes who should be worried. The hard part of replacing a mature system is not writing the new code; it is establishing what the old system does, which of those behaviours are contract and which are accident. That is product work. When a PM says "the rewrite is an engineering matter", they have volunteered the project for its most common cause of death.

"We can't move fast because of debt" is often "we can't move fast because of coordination"

Before accepting the diagnosis, measure where time actually goes. In many teams, a feature with three weeks of hands-on-keyboard work takes eleven weeks elapsed, and the missing eight are queueing: waiting for review, for a dependent team, for a release window, for a decision. A rewrite fixes none of that, and teams that rewrite when their real problem is flow discover their cycle time unchanged on the new stack.

Conway's law applies to replacements too

Melvin Conway observed in 1968 that systems tend to mirror the communication structure of the organisations that build them. If the reason the pricing logic exists in three forks is that three teams could never agree a schedule to merge it, then a rewrite performed by those same three teams will produce three new forks within eighteen months. Rewriting code without changing ownership boundaries is an expensive way to reproduce your org chart in a newer language.

What the idea cannot tell you

The debt frame prices the cost of the status quo. It says nothing about whether the product should exist, whether the market will still want it in three years, or how volatile the domain is. A start-up whose product-market fit is uncertain has a very high discount rate on its own future: debt due in four years may never come due at all. A company with ninety-one contracted customers and eighty per cent gross retention, like Bhramar, has a low discount rate and should take long-dated costs seriously. Same code, different answer.

The questions to ask before relying on any of this

Four, in order. Who is paying the interest right now — which team, on which roadmap items, by name? What is the smallest slice that would prove the remedy works, and when would we know? What happens if we cancel at the halfway point — do we keep anything? And who will delete the old code, on what date? A plan with no answer to the last question is not a replacement plan; it is a plan to run two systems forever.

SixHow the shape changes with product and stage

In consumer products the interest often shows up as a release-cadence problem rather than a feature-cost problem. Bahaar Beauty, a Mumbai consumer commerce app competing in the category Nykaa defined, can ship a feature quickly but cannot experiment quickly: its checkout code cannot support two variants at once, so every pricing test requires a sequential release. The cost is not engineer-weeks; it is learning rate. A consumer company that runs 40 experiments a quarter instead of 120 is paying its interest in forgone knowledge, which no time-tracking exercise will reveal.

In B2B the interest is usually concentrated in configurability and in the support organisation. Bhramar's per-customer forks are the classic form: the debt sits not in the core but in the ninety-one variations, and its cost appears on the services P&L, not engineering's. The PM who only reads engineering's numbers will systematically under-price B2B debt.

In marketplaces the debt is entangled with market outcomes. Bhadra Bazaar, an Ahmedabad marketplace for building materials, has a matching service whose quirks have become the rules by which its 6,000 suppliers earn. Replacing it is not a neutral engineering act: a "cleaner" matcher redistributes income, and suppliers who lose will call. Bug-for-bug compatibility is a commercial decision, and the PM must decide, behaviour by behaviour, which quirks are contract.

Stage matters more than most frameworks admit. In a fifteen-person company, taking deliberate debt is usually correct, because the probability of the code mattering in three years is low and the cost of slowness now is existential. In a 600-person company the calculation reverses: the debt is loaded onto teams that did not take it, in code they did not write, and the compounding horizon is long. What does not change is the register: name the module, price the interest, state the maturity.

SevenFour ways this decision routinely goes wrong

The quality quarter

The symptom, visible from outside: a quarter is branded as a clean-up quarter, and at the end of it nobody can name a number that moved. The misunderstanding is that debt work is a category of activity rather than an investment with a return. The cheapest diagnostic is one question asked before the quarter starts: which measurement will be different in March, and what is it today? If no one can answer, the quarter will produce tidier code and identical cycle times.

The rewrite with no cutover plan

The symptom is a project plan whose penultimate step is "migrate customers" and whose duration for that step is a round number. The misunderstanding is that cutover is an event rather than the hardest, longest phase. The diagnostic: ask what happens if the project is cancelled in month five. If the answer is "we'd have nothing", it is a big-bang rewrite whatever it is called, and the honest risk-adjusted cost is the one with the 1.8× multiplier on it.

Proxy metrics standing in for interest

The symptom is a debt conversation conducted in code-coverage percentages, static-analysis grades or a count of "debt tickets". The misunderstanding is that these measure cost; they measure correlates of cost, and they are gameable, which means over time they will be gamed. The diagnostic is to ask for one planned roadmap item, by name, and the estimate difference attributable to the debt. If the team cannot connect the metric to a date on the roadmap, the metric is decoration.

The PM who treats debt as engineering's business

The symptom is a fixed percentage — "twenty per cent for tech debt" — that is raided whenever a quarter goes badly, which is to say always. The misunderstanding is that a percentage is a decision; it is an abdication of one. The diagnostic: ask the PM which specific roadmap commitment the debt endangers, with a date. A PM who can answer that has priced the debt into the plan, and the allocation argument dissolves.

EightWhat good looks like

Handled well, this decision looks unremarkable. The team keeps a register like the one above and reviews it monthly, in the same meeting as the roadmap, not in a separate engineering forum. Every item carries an interest estimate, a maturity, a proposed slice and a named owner. Debt work appears on the roadmap with the same visibility as features, described in the language of what it unlocks: not "refactor the allocation engine" but "reduce the cost of a new picking strategy from eleven weeks to three, so that quick-commerce deals close in-quarter." And every replacement plan has a decommission date for the old code, with a person's name against it, because the most expensive outcome in this entire field is not a failed rewrite — it is a successful one that never deletes what it replaced.

NineWhat Ananya decided

She did not approve the rewrite, and she did not refuse it. On 26 March 2026 she proposed to Sudha a twenty-week replacement of strategy selection alone, with Farida Sheikh as technical lead and a product manager assigned full-time to requirements archaeology: enumerating, from the 2,400 branches and four years of support tickets, which behaviours were contract and which were accident. The new component would run in shadow mode against live traffic for three weeks before any customer was moved, then take one customer, then twelve, then all. Nikhil kept his design; he lost his scope and his schedule, and gained the thing he actually wanted, which was for the next five picking strategies to take three weeks instead of eleven. The batch-picking deal was quoted at fourteen weeks rather than eleven, because the first slice had to land first — a cost Ananya accepted openly rather than concealed.

Her reasoning, stated in one line to the board: the company was paying ₹98 lakh a year in interest, 77 per cent of it on 8 per cent of the code, and there was no version of the argument in which it made sense to spend ₹2.57 crore and nine months of roadmap to address all of it at once.

What to learn next follows directly. Cost, quality and time trade-offs gives the general form of the argument this topic is a special case of. Migrations and rebuilds covers the mechanics of cutover — dual-write, shadow reads, reconciliation, decommissioning — which is where replacement projects actually fail. Strategic debt takes the other side seriously: how to take debt deliberately, price it at the moment you take it, and record it so that the person who inherits it knows what was traded and why.

Two questions to sit with.

1. Bhramar's register says the tenant-configuration module carries only nine engineer-weeks of annual interest, and so is not worth remediating — but only one engineer can read it. What is the right way to price the risk that Farida Sheikh resigns, and does it belong in this register at all or in a different one?

2. Suppose Nikhil is right that the allocation engine's architecture makes the batch-picking feature genuinely impossible rather than merely expensive — not eleven weeks but never. Which parts of the analysis above survive that claim, and what evidence would you require before believing it?
