Gautami Systems: Rewrite or Build On?

Bengaluru, 3 March 2025

On the last Monday of the Bengaluru winter, Ananya Rao stood at the window of Gautami Systems' fourth-floor office on Sarjapur Road, watching the traffic thicken on the flyover, and read for the third time the email from the company's board. The Series C term sheet was signed, subject to two weeks of technical due diligence beginning 17 March. The diligence partner, a former Flipkart engineering director now advising the lead investor, had asked a single pointed question in his introductory call: "Your release velocity has halved in eighteen months while your incident count has tripled. What is your engineering roadmap, and what does it cost?" Ananya, Vice President of Product at Gautami, had eleven days to bring her co-founder and the rest of the leadership team to one answer, and to write it down for the board.

1. The company

Gautami Systems was founded in 2016 by Karthik Subramaniam and a college friend, two IIT Madras graduates who had watched India's D2C boom outgrow the spreadsheets and WhatsApp groups that young sellers were using to track stock. Their product, Saral, was an order-management and inventory-reconciliation platform: it sat between a brand's warehouse and the marketplaces it sold on — Flipkart, Meesho, Amazon, and increasingly the ONDC network — updating stock levels, routing orders to the nearest fulfilment centre, and reconciling payouts. Saral's natural competitors were Unicommerce, Increff and Vinculum Solutions, all of whom had been in the market longer and had deeper enterprise sales relationships. Gautami's edge, in its early years, had been speed: it shipped integrations faster than anyone, sometimes within days of a marketplace changing its API, because its founding engineers had built a lean, fast-moving monolith and were willing to hand-patch it at midnight during a big sale.

By early 2025 Saral processed inventory and order data for 340 D2C and quick-commerce sellers, spanning categories from beauty and personal care to consumer electronics — the kind of sellers who competed for shelf space alongside brands like Nykaa's marketplace partners, boAt's D2C channel and Lenskart's omnichannel stores. Annual recurring revenue stood at roughly ₹38 crore, growing 60% year on year, and the company employed 58 engineers split across Bengaluru and Pune, with product, design and data functions scattered further still. The same monolith that had made Gautami fast in 2017 was, by 2025, the thing every senior engineer wanted to talk about first in any all-hands.

2. The situation

The strain had been building for two years. Every marketplace integration, every GST e-invoicing rule change, every new payment reconciliation format had been added as a module bolted onto the original order-processing core, because bolting on was always faster than redesigning, and Gautami had never had a quarter where it felt safe to slow down. Karthik, now CTO and based in Pune, had asked twice before for a dedicated rewrite quarter and been told, both times, that the sales pipeline could not absorb a feature freeze. Meera Krishnan, the Bengaluru-based engineering manager who ran the on-call rotation, could recite the pattern from memory: a bug fix in the reconciliation module would quietly break the returns module, because both wrote to the same order-state table without either being fully aware of the other's assumptions. The exhibits below, compiled by Meera for the board pack, showed the trend in numbers rather than anecdotes (Exhibit 1).

The decision had a sharper edge because of two things arriving at once. The first was the Series C diligence itself, which would look hardest at whether engineering could scale with revenue. The second was a renewal conversation with Gautami's largest single account, Al Meraaj Retail Group, a Dubai-based multi-category retailer that ran twelve storefronts across the UAE and Saudi Arabia on Saral and was worth ₹6.4 crore in annual revenue — about a sixth of the company's ARR. Al Meraaj's regional IT head had told Rachel Lim, Gautami's Singapore-based customer success lead who managed the account across a three-hour time difference from Dubai and a five-and-a-half-hour one from Bengaluru, that the retailer needed a contractual 99.9% inventory-sync uptime commitment by the contract renewal in Q3, after two embarrassing stock-outs during Ramadan sales had reached their category head's desk. Rachel's message to Ananya was blunt: whatever the engineering roadmap looked like, it could not include a quarter where Al Meraaj's integration was untouched or unstable.

Ananya's task, concretely, was to recommend one of three paths to the founders and the board within eleven days, in a document that would also serve as the technical roadmap section of the diligence response.

3. The people

Karthik Subramaniam — Co-founder and CTO, Pune. Wants a clean, dedicated rewrite of the order-orchestration core. He believes the company is one bad Big Billion Days-style peak away from a catastrophic multi-hour outage, and that continuing to patch the monolith is now more expensive, in engineering hours, than starting over.
Priyanka Chatterjee — Data Scientist, Toronto. Builds Saral's demand-forecasting feature, a differentiator the sales team wants to sell hard into the US market. She is blocked repeatedly by the legacy core's inconsistent order-state data, and wants an investment in a clean data layer, though not necessarily a full rewrite of everything above it.
Rachel Lim — Customer Success Lead, Singapore. Owns the Al Meraaj relationship and eleven other large accounts. She wants stability and visible incremental improvement, and is wary of any plan that takes engineering attention away from the current platform for months at a stretch.
Grant Michaels — Head of Sales, New Jersey. Is building a pipeline of US-market deals that need multi-currency support and faster onboarding, features that a feature freeze would delay. He argues the Series C story is a growth story, and growth needs visible new capability, not an invisible rewrite.

4. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 was the number Meera used to open every roadmap conversation: engineering headcount had more than tripled since FY22, yet quarterly releases had fallen by nearly two-thirds and the share of engineering time spent simply keeping the existing system upright had risen from about a fifth to well over half. Karthik's reading was straightforward — Gautami was now paying, in salary, for a growing team whose majority effort produced no new customer value, and the trend line, if extended, implied the company would be nearly fully absorbed by upkeep within eighteen months.

5. The options

A. Rewrite the core

Freeze major new features on the order-orchestration core for roughly seven months and rebuild it with clean service boundaries, at an estimated ₹4.2 crore. The upside is a platform Karthik believes could sustain five years of growth without another crisis, and a strong, specific answer to the diligence partner's question. The cost is real: a freeze during precisely the quarter Al Meraaj wants visible stability, and a sales team with a quieter product story for the US pipeline just as the Series C closes.

B. Build on: strangler-fig refactor

Wrap the legacy core in new services one module at a time — starting with the reconciliation and returns modules that generate the most incidents — while continuing to ship customer-facing features at a reduced pace, over roughly fourteen months at ₹2.9 crore. This is slower to reach a fully clean architecture and carries the risk of running two systems side by side for over a year, doubling certain classes of bugs during the transition. Its upside is that no quarter is a lost quarter: Al Meraaj sees continuous improvement, and Grant's US pipeline keeps receiving features, even if more slowly.

C. Patch critical modules and defer

Fund targeted fixes only to the reconciliation and returns modules most implicated in P1 incidents, at roughly ₹85 lakh, and leave the broader rewrite question for after the Series C closes and the company can raise a dedicated engineering budget. This preserves feature velocity for the fundraise and the US pipeline in the short term, but Exhibit 1's trend line does not reverse — it is likely to continue, and the risk of a severe outage during a peak sale season, such as the festive period around Diwali, keeps compounding rather than shrinking.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. What, precisely, does Exhibit 1 show is happening to Gautami's engineering capacity, and by when does the trend become unsustainable if nothing changes?
  2. Each stakeholder — Karthik, Priyanka, Rachel and Grant — is reasoning from a real constraint. What is each person's constraint, and where do their preferred paths conflict with each other?
  3. How should the Al Meraaj renewal and the Series C diligence timeline change the relative weight Ananya gives to speed versus stability in her recommendation?
  4. Of the three options, which one best balances the cost of technical debt against the cost of paying it down all at once, and what would make you change your answer?

7. A note for the learner

Technical debt is a useful metaphor precisely because it behaves like financial debt: it lets a team borrow speed today against interest paid in engineering hours tomorrow, and like financial debt, a small amount taken on deliberately is often a good decision, while debt that accumulates without anyone tracking the interest rate becomes dangerous. The classic PM–engineering conflict is not that one side is right and the other wrong; it is that product and engineering are, by default, measuring different things — product tracks features shipped and revenue at risk, engineering tracks the compounding cost of each additional change to a fragile system — and neither number alone tells Ananya what to do. A well-reasoned answer treats Exhibit 1 as the debt's interest rate becoming visible, and treats Exhibit 3 as three different repayment plans, not three different attitudes toward risk.

The case is built so that Option C, patch and defer, can be set aside quickly: Exhibit 1's trend line shows that upkeep is already consuming more than half of engineering time and rising, and deferring the decision does not pause that trend, it extends it into a fundraising narrative that the diligence partner has already signalled he will scrutinise closely. That leaves a genuine choice between A and B, and the case favours Option B, the strangler-fig refactor, as the more defensible path — not because rewrites are always wrong, but because Gautami has two live commitments, the Al Meraaj renewal and the Series C growth story, that a hard feature freeze would jeopardise in the same quarter the company can least afford it. A phased refactor lets Ananya tell the board a coherent story: engineering time on legacy upkeep falls steadily rather than all at once, Rachel can show Al Meraaj visible, incremental reliability gains against the 99.9% target well before the Q3 renewal, and Grant's US pipeline keeps receiving new capability, even if more slowly than he would like. The defensible reasoning is not "avoid the rewrite" but "sequence the debt paydown against the commitments already made" — the same discipline a good CFO applies to refinancing, borrowing against future stability rather than freezing the business to pay everything down today.
